exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 21–30, $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ for some vector $$\textbf{x}$$ , then $$\text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ .
(T/F) If $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ for some scalar $$\text{λ}$$ , then $$\textbf{x}$$ is an eigenvector of $$A$$ .
(T/F) A matrix $$A$$ is invertible if and only if $$0$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ .
(T/F) A number $$c$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ if and only if the equation $$(A - cI)\textbf{x} = 0$$ has a nontrivial solution.
(T/F) Finding an eigenvector of $$A$$ may be difficult, but checking whether a given vector is in fact an eigenvector is easy.
(T/F) To find the eigenvalues of $$A$$ , reduce $$A$$ to echelon form.
(T/F) If $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ are linearly independent eigenvectors, then they correspond to distinct eigenvalues.
(T/F) The eigenvalues of a matrix are on its main diagonal.
(T/F) If $$\textbf{v}$$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $$2$$ , then $$2\textbf{v}$$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $$4$$ .
(T/F) An eigenspace of $$A$$ is a null space of a certain matrix.
Explain why a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix can have at most two distinct eigenvalues. Explain why an $$n \times n$$ matrix can have at most $$n$$ distinct eigenvalues.
Construct an example of a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix with only one distinct eigenvalue.

Let $$\text{λ}$$ be an eigenvalue of an invertible matrix $$A$$ . Show that $$\text{λ} ^{- 1}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A^{- 1}$$ . [Hint: Suppose a nonzero $$\textbf{x}$$ satisfies $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ .]
Show that if $$A^{2}$$ is the zero matrix, then the only eigenvalue of $$A$$ is $$0$$ .
Show that $$\text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ if and only if $$\text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A^{T}$$ . [Hint: Find out how $$A - \text{λ} I$$ and $$A^{T} - \text{λ} I$$ are related.]
Use Exercise 35 to complete the proof of Theorem 1 for the case when $$A$$ is lower triangular.
Consider an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ with the property that the row sums all equal the same number $$s$$ . Show that $$s$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ . [Hint: Find an eigenvector.]
Consider an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ with the property that the column sums all equal the same number $$s$$ . Show that $$s$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ . [Hint: Use Exercises 35 and 37.]

problem.paragraph: The number $$5$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ if and only if the equation $$(A - 5I)\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has a nontrivial solution. Form $$A - 51 = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & - 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & 5 \\ 2 & 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 1 \\ 3 & - 5 & 5 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

and row reduce the augmented matrix: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & - 5 & 5 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & - 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & - 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
At this point, it is clear that the homogeneous system has no free variables. Thus $$A - 5I$$ is an invertible matrix, which means that $$5$$ is not an eigenvalue of $$A$$ .

If $$\textbf{x}$$ is an eigenvector of $$A$$ corresponding to $$\text{λ}$$ , then $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ and so $$A^{2} x = A \left(\right. \lambda x \left.\right) = \lambda A x = \lambda^{2} x$$

Again, $$A^{3}\textbf{x} = A(A^{2}\textbf{x}) = A( \text{λ} ^{2}\textbf{x}) = \text{λ} ^{2}A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} ^{3}\textbf{x}$$ . The general pattern, $$A^{k} \textbf{x} =$$ $$\text{λ} ^{k}\textbf{x}$$ , is proved by induction.

Yes. Suppose $$c_{1}\textbf{b}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{b}_{2} + (c_{3}\textbf{b}_{3} + c_{4}\textbf{b}_{4}) = \textbf{0}$$ . Since any linear combination of eigenvectors corresponding to the same eigenvalue is in the eigenspace for that eigenvalue, $$c_{3}\textbf{b}_{3} + c_{4}\textbf{b}_{4}$$ is either $$0$$ or an eigenvector for $$\text{λ} _{3}$$ . If $$c_{3}\textbf{b}_{3} + c_{4}\textbf{b}_{4}$$ were an eigenvector for $$\text{λ} _{3}$$ , then by Theorem 2, $$\{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2},c_{3}\textbf{b}_{3} + c_{4}\textbf{b}_{4}\}$$ would be a linearly independent set, which would force $$c_{1} = c_{2} = 0$$ and $$c_{3}\textbf{b}_{3} + c_{4}\textbf{b}_{4} = \textbf{0}$$ , contradicting that $$c_{3}\textbf{b}_{3} + c_{4}\textbf{b}_{4}$$ is an eigenvector. Thus $$c_{3}\textbf{b}_{3} + c_{4}\textbf{b}_{4}$$ must be 0, implying that $$c_{1}\textbf{b}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{b}_{2} = \textbf{0}$$ also. By Theorem 2, $$\{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2}\}$$ is a linearly independent set so $$c_{1} = c_{2} = 0$$ . Moreover, $$\{\textbf{b}_{3},\textbf{b}_{4}\}$$ is a linearly independent set so $$c_{3} = c_{4} = 0$$ . Since all of the coefficients $$c_{1}$$ , $$c_{2}$$ , $$c_{3}$$ , and $$c_{4}$$ must be zero, it follows that $$\left\{ \textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2},\textbf{b}_{3},\textbf{b}_{4} \right\}$$ is a linearly independent set.

Since $$\text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ , there is a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\textbf{R}^{n}$$ such that $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ . Multiplying both sides of this equation by $$2$$ results in the equation $$2(A\textbf{x}) = 2( \text{λ} \textbf{x})$$ . Thus $$(2A)\textbf{x} = (2 \text{λ} )\textbf{x}$$ and hence $$2 \text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$2A$$ .
